title: Inequity in social exchange
venue: In L. Berkowitz (Ed.), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, Vol. 2, pp. 267–299. Academic Press
finding: Founding statement of equity theory: people compare the ratio of what they put in to what they get out with someone else’s, and feel tension when the ratios differ.
strength: strong — foundational and well supported in workplace research; more mixed in close relationships
note: DOI confirmed only via two reference lists, not the publisher page.

authors: Walster, E. [Hatfield, E.], Walster, G. W., & Berscheid, E.
title: Equity: Theory and Research
finding: Extended equity theory to close relationships: feeling under-benefited goes with anger and resentment, feeling over-benefited with guilt, and both with less satisfaction than feeling things are roughly fair.
strength: moderate — influential; in loving relationships the evidence is more mixed than at work
note: Author listed as Hatfield (formerly Walster) on her own publications page; the book is often cited as Walster, Walster & Berscheid (1978).

authors: Walster, E., Berscheid, E., & Walster, G. W.
title: New directions in equity research
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 25, 151–176
finding: Set out the four propositions of equity theory used in later relationship research.
strength: moderate — classic theoretical paper
note: Citation details confirmed by reference lists, but no DOI or landing page was confirmed. Optional companion to the 1978 book; do not link until the DOI is checked.

title: Interpersonal attraction in exchange and communal relationships
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(1), 12–24
finding: Distinguished communal relationships (benefits given in response to needs) from exchange relationships (benefits given in return for benefits). When people wanted a communal relationship, being repaid in kind reduced attraction.
strength: strong — two experiments, widely replicated distinction
note: Title, authors, year, journal, volume and pages confirmed (PDF on the Clark lab site). The DOI follows the APA pattern for this volume and issue but was not shown in a search result, so the link uses the lab-hosted PDF.

authors: Hochschild, A. R., with Machung, A.
title: The Second Shift: Working Parents and the Revolution at Home
finding: Interviews and home observations of dual-earner couples with young children found that working mothers did much more of the housework and childcare, adding up to a large extra load over a year; many couples told themselves stories that the split was fair.
strength: moderate — influential qualitative study; its figures describe its sample, though large time-use surveys confirm a persistent (narrowing) gap

title: The Managed Heart: Commercialization of Human Feeling
finding: Coined “emotional labor” from a study of flight attendants (and bill collectors) trained to display feelings at work; distinguished surface acting from deep acting.
strength: strong as a concept — later meta-analyses link surface acting with exhaustion; family “emotion work” research is smaller
note: No publisher page surfaced in search; swap in the University of California Press page if available.

title: The cognitive dimension of household labor
finding: Interviews with 35 couples (70 interviews) identified four parts of household “cognitive labor”: anticipating needs, identifying options, deciding, and monitoring. Women did more of it overall, especially anticipating and monitoring; deciding was shared more equally. The work was often unseen by both partners.
strength: moderate — rich qualitative study of a mostly college-educated sample; not population estimates

title: Invisible work
finding: Argued that everyday definitions of “work” leave out a great deal of effortful activity, especially unpaid domestic and volunteer work, so it goes unrecognised.
strength: moderate — a conceptual framework supported by many qualitative studies rather than a single measurable variable

title: The female world of cards and holidays: Women, families, and the work of kinship
venue: Signs: Journal of Women in Culture and Society, 12(3), 440–453
finding: Named “kin work”: the cards, calls, visits, gifts and gatherings that keep extended families connected. In the families she studied, it was done mostly by women and often treated as effortless.
strength: moderate — influential anthropological study; qualitative

title: Egocentric biases in availability and attribution
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(3), 322–336
finding: In five experiments (married couples, groups, basketball teams), people recalled more of their own contributions to joint work and took more responsibility than others gave them; spouses’ estimates of their own shares typically summed to more than 100 percent.
strength: strong — classic, widely replicated

authors: Caruso, E. M., Epley, N., & Bazerman, M. H.
title: The costs and benefits of undoing egocentric responsibility assessments in groups
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 91(5), 857–871
finding: Group members (including academic co-authors) overstated their own share of the work; thinking about others’ contributions reduced the bias, but high contributors then felt less satisfied with the collaboration.
strength: moderate — several experiments; shows that perspective-taking has costs as well as benefits

authors: Carlson, D. L., Miller, A. J., Sassler, S., & Hanson, S.
title: The gendered division of housework and couples’ sexual relationships: A reexamination
finding: Using 2006 survey data, egalitarian couples had sex as often, and were as satisfied with it, as conventional couples, unlike an earlier study based on older data; couples where the man did most of the housework reported less frequent and lower-quality sex.
strength: moderate — one US sample of mostly lower- to middle-income couples with children; correlational
note: Volume/issue/pages from a faculty listing; DOI not confirmed. The GSU link is a repository copy (earlier working-paper version).

title: Research on household labor: Modeling and measuring the social embeddedness of routine family work
finding: A major review of household-labor research: how gender, paid work, income and attitudes shape who does routine family work, and how the division links to perceived fairness and wellbeing.
strength: strong — widely cited review; representative source for the “long line of studies” the site mentions
note: The site names Coltrane among researchers but cites no specific work; this review is offered as the read-more link.

title: The allocation of household labor by partners in gay and lesbian couples
finding: Among 43 gay and 36 lesbian couples where both partners worked full-time, household tasks were divided more evenly than is typical in heterosexual couples, often by negotiation and specialisation rather than gender.
strength: moderate — small, non-random samples; consistent with other studies of same-sex couples
note: Pages 132–148 not shown in the search result (volume/year/DOI were).

authors: Yavorsky, J. E., Kamp Dush, C. M., & Schoppe-Sullivan, S. J.
title: The production of inequality: The gender division of labor across the transition to parenthood
finding: Time-diary data from dual-earner couples showed a gender gap in total work opening up after a first baby: mothers took on most of the added childcare without cutting their paid hours; survey reports overstated how equal things were.
strength: moderate — careful longitudinal design; small, highly educated US sample
note: Representative source for the site’s unattributed claim that the split “often becomes more traditional” after a first baby (book/chapter-2-in-depth.html#trend).

authors: Allen, S. M., & Hawkins, A. J.
title: Maternal gatekeeping: Mothers’ beliefs and behaviors that inhibit greater father involvement in family work
venue: Journal of Marriage and the Family, 61(1), 199–212
finding: Defined maternal gatekeeping along three dimensions and, in 622 dual-earner mothers, classified about one in five as gatekeepers; they did more family work each week and had less equal divisions of labor.
strength: moderate — influential concept; later work stresses both gate-closing and gate-opening and warns against blaming mothers

authors: Schoppe-Sullivan, S. J., Brown, G. L., Cannon, E. A., Mangelsdorf, S. C., & Sokolowski, M. S.
title: Maternal gatekeeping, coparenting quality, and fathering behavior in families with infants
finding: In 97 couples with infants, fathers were more involved in day-to-day care when mothers actively encouraged them (gate-opening); when mothers were highly critical (gate-closing), fathers’ own beliefs about involvement mattered less.
strength: moderate — observational study of one US sample; correlational

authors: Gordon, A. M., Impett, E. A., Kogan, A., Oveis, C., & Keltner, D.
title: To have and to hold: Gratitude promotes relationship maintenance in intimate bonds
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(2), 257–274
finding: People who felt more appreciated by their romantic partners were more appreciative of their partners in return, and appreciation was linked with relationship maintenance and commitment.
strength: moderate — several studies including longitudinal data; correlational

title: Equity, equality, and need: What determines which value will be used as the basis of distributive justice?
finding: Argued that equity is only one of several justice principles, alongside equality and need, and proposed when groups favour each: equality in cooperative relationships, equity in economic ones, need in caring ones.
strength: moderate — influential theory; research broadly supports that the chosen principle depends on context
note: DOI not confirmed; link is a GESIS bibliographic record. Replace with the Wiley page if found.

title: Procedural Justice: A Psychological Analysis
finding: Founded procedural-justice research: people’s judgments of whether a decision process is fair (especially having a voice) shape how satisfied they are with the outcome.
strength: strong — one of the more robust findings in social and organizational psychology, though early lab methods were criticised

title: Fairness heuristic theory: Justice judgments as pivotal cognitions in organizational relations
venue: In J. Greenberg & R. Cropanzano (Eds.), Advances in Organizational Justice (pp. 56–88). Stanford University Press
finding: Proposed that people use fair treatment as a mental shortcut when deciding whether to trust and cooperate with an authority or group.
strength: moderate — influential theory with supporting experiments
note: Link is a library catalogue record for the edited volume.

authors: Papp, L. M., Cummings, E. M., & Goeke-Morey, M. C.
title: For richer, for poorer: Money as a topic of marital conflict in the home
finding: In home diary records of marital conflict, money was not the most frequent topic, but money conflicts were more pervasive, problematic and recurrent than other conflicts and more likely to stay unresolved.
strength: moderate — diary design with one US community sample; correlational

authors: Dew, J., Britt, S., & Huston, S.
title: Examining the relationship between financial issues and divorce
finding: In US national survey data on about 4,500 couples, financial disagreements were the strongest of the disagreement types in predicting later divorce, for both wives and husbands.
strength: moderate — large longitudinal sample; correlational
note: DOI shown by one source only; link uses the BYU repository copy.

authors: Rick, S. I., Small, D. A., & Finkel, E. J.
title: Fatal (fiscal) attraction: Spendthrifts and tightwads in marriage
finding: Tightwads and spendthrifts tend to marry each other; the bigger the difference within a couple, the more conflict over money, which in turn predicts lower marital wellbeing.
strength: moderate — several survey studies; correlational

authors: Klontz, B., Britt, S. L., Mentzer, J., & Klontz, T.
title: Money beliefs and financial behaviors: Development of the Klontz Money Script Inventory
finding: In 422 respondents, beliefs about money clustered into four “money scripts” (money avoidance, money worship, money status and money vigilance), several of which were linked with income and net worth.
strength: early — a newer measure from one sample; the site rightly calls it “less established”

authors: Conger, R. D., Elder, G. H., Jr., Lorenz, F. O., Conger, K. J., Simons, R. L., Whitbeck, L. B., Huck, S., & Melby, J. N.
title: Linking economic hardship to marital quality and instability
venue: Journal of Marriage and the Family, 52(3), 643–656
finding: In 76 rural Midwestern couples, financial pressure lowered marital quality indirectly, by increasing hostility and reducing warmth between spouses; this became a basis for the Family Stress Model.
strength: moderate — small, homogeneous sample; the model has since been widely tested
note: JSTOR stable ID 352931 as reported by search; DOI not confirmed. The site names Conger’s economic-hardship work without a specific paper; this is the representative source.

title: The internal structure and ecological context of coparenting: A framework for research and intervention
finding: Set out a framework for coparenting (how parents work together as parents) with components such as childrearing agreement, support versus undermining, division of labor, and joint family management.
strength: moderate — influential framework that guided later trials

authors: Feinberg, M. E., & Kan, M. L.
title: Establishing Family Foundations: Intervention effects on coparenting, parent/infant well-being, and parent-child relations
finding: A randomized trial with 169 expectant first-time couples found that the Family Foundations classes, delivered before and after birth, improved coparenting and some aspects of parent and infant wellbeing at follow-up.
strength: moderate — randomized trial; later trials broadly supportive

title: Effects of authoritative parental control on child behavior
finding: Described authoritarian, authoritative and permissive styles of parental control, arguing for “authoritative” parenting that combines warmth with firm, explained limits.
strength: strong as a framework — many studies link authoritative parenting with good outcomes, mostly in Western, middle-class samples

authors: Maccoby, E. E., & Martin, J. A.
title: Socialization in the context of the family: Parent–child interaction
venue: In P. H. Mussen (Ed.), Handbook of Child Psychology, Vol. 4: Socialization, Personality, and Social Development (pp. 1–102). Wiley
finding: A major review that recast parenting styles along two dimensions, responsiveness and demandingness, adding a neglectful/uninvolved style to Baumrind’s three.
strength: strong as a framework — widely used; styles are broad descriptions rather than precise categories
note: Link is a library catalogue record; the volume editor (Hetherington) is from general knowledge and not shown in the search result.

authors: Doss, B. D., Rhoades, G. K., Stanley, S. M., & Markman, H. J.
title: The effect of the transition to parenthood on relationship quality: An 8-year prospective study
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 96(3), 601–619
finding: Following 218 couples over the first eight years of marriage, those who had a first child showed sudden declines in relationship quality after the birth, on average, compared with couples who did not.
strength: moderate — strong longitudinal design; averages hide wide variation

authors: Twenge, J. M., Campbell, W. K., & Foster, C. A.
title: Parenthood and marital satisfaction: A meta-analytic review
finding: Across studies, parents reported lower marital satisfaction than non-parents, with the gap largest among mothers of infants.
strength: moderate — meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional studies; a later meta-analysis (Mitnick et al., 2009) found smaller effects

authors: Cowan, C. P., & Cowan, P. A.
title: When Partners Become Parents: The Big Life Change for Couples
finding: Based on the Becoming a Family Project, a long-term study of expectant couples, describes how strain and conflict between partners commonly rise across the transition to parenthood, and tests couples groups as prevention.
strength: moderate — longitudinal study with a preventive intervention; modest sample

title: Surviving and Thriving in Stepfamily Relationships: What Works and What Doesn’t
finding: Describes “stepfamily architecture” and five common challenges it creates, drawing on research and clinical experience; closeness between stepfamily members typically builds slowly.
strength: moderate — practitioner synthesis of research and clinical experience, not a single study

title: Stepfamily Relationships: Development, Dynamics, and Interventions (2nd ed.)
finding: A research-based overview of stepfamily relationships, covering how they form and change, common dynamics, and interventions.
strength: strong — scholarly synthesis by leading stepfamily researchers
note: The site names Ganong and Coleman without a specific work; this book is the representative source.

title: For Better or For Worse: Divorce Reconsidered
finding: Drawing on long-term studies of about 1,400 families, argues that most children of divorce and remarriage turn out reasonably well, with outcomes varying widely.
strength: moderate — large longitudinal programme; popular book that drew some controversy
note: The site names Hetherington without a specific work; this book is the representative source.

title: Children of divorce in the 1990s: An update of the Amato and Keith (1991) meta-analysis
finding: Updated a meta-analysis comparing children of divorced and continuously married parents; differences in wellbeing were small on average and persisted in studies from the 1990s.
strength: strong — meta-analysis; correlational studies
note: DOI from one reference list; end page shown as 370 in most sources (one says 365). Representative source for deep.json “Robert Emery, Paul Amato and others”.

title: Interparental conflict and the children of discord and divorce
finding: Reviewed evidence that conflict between parents, in married and divorced families, is linked to children’s problems, and that the amount and type of conflict matter.
strength: strong — classic review
note: Citation (author, year, title, journal, volume, pages) confirmed from reference lists, but no DOI or landing page was confirmed. Likely DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.92.2.310 — check before linking.

title: Differences between caregivers and noncaregivers in psychological health and physical health: A meta-analysis
finding: Across 84 studies, caregivers reported more stress and depression and lower wellbeing and self-efficacy than non-caregivers, with smaller differences in physical health; gaps were larger for dementia caregivers.
strength: strong — large meta-analysis; correlational

authors: Suitor, J. J., Gilligan, M., Johnson, K., & Pillemer, K.
title: Caregiving, perceptions of maternal favoritism, and tension among siblings
finding: Examined how sibling tension when a parent needs care relates to which sibling takes on caregiving and to perceptions that the mother favours some children.
strength: moderate — survey of US families; correlational
note: Published online 2013; print issue 2014. Representative source for the site’s “Jill Suitor and Karl Pillemer” sibling-caregiving mention.

title: Fault Lines: Fractured Families and How to Mend Them
finding: Draws on the Cornell Reconciliation Project, including a national survey on estrangement and interviews, to show family estrangement is more common than people assume and that some people reconcile.
strength: moderate — survey plus interviews; popular book

title: Family Evaluation: An Approach Based on Bowen Theory
finding: Explains Bowen family systems theory (differentiation, triangles, roles passed across generations) and how to evaluate a family as an emotional unit.
strength: debated — influential in family therapy; limited empirical testing

title: Rewriting Family Scripts: Improvisation and Systems Change
finding: Describes “family scripts” (repeated, often inherited patterns of interaction) and how families can rewrite them from a “secure family base”, drawing on attachment research.
strength: early — clinical framework, supported more by clinical experience than experiments

authors: Laursen, B., Coy, K. C., & Collins, W. A.
title: Reconsidering changes in parent-child conflict across adolescence: A meta-analysis
finding: Parent–child conflict became less frequent with age across adolescence, while the emotional intensity of conflicts rose from early to mid-adolescence.
strength: strong — meta-analysis
note: DOI from one source; PubMed link used.

authors: Roskam, I., Raes, M.-E., & Mikolajczak, M.
title: Exhausted parents: Development and preliminary validation of the Parental Burnout Inventory
finding: Developed a 22-item Parental Burnout Inventory with three factors (exhaustion, inefficacy and emotional distancing from one’s children), only moderately related to job burnout, parenting stress and depression.
strength: early — a fast-growing field; measurement still being refined

authors: Bryant, C. M., Conger, R. D., & Meehan, J. M.
title: The influence of in-laws on change in marital success
finding: Longitudinal study of how relationships with in-laws relate to changes in marital success over time.
strength: moderate — longitudinal; correlational
note: Citation confirmed only from later reference lists; the paper’s own findings and a DOI/landing page were not confirmed. Candidate source for the site’s unattributed in-law claims — do not link until checked.

authors: Greenhaus, J. H., & Beutell, N. J.
title: Sources of conflict between work and family roles
finding: Reviewed the literature and described three forms of work–family conflict: time-based, strain-based and behaviour-based.
strength: strong — foundational model; meta-analyses link work–family conflict with lower satisfaction
note: DOI not confirmed; link is the Drexel repository record.

title: Effects of daily workload on subsequent behavior during marital interaction: The roles of social withdrawal and spouse support
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 57(4), 651–659
finding: In a daily study of air traffic controllers, after high-workload days they were more socially withdrawn and less emotionally expressive with their spouses that evening.
strength: moderate — small daily-diary study; an early classic of “spillover” research
note: DOI not confirmed; link is the PDF on the UCLA psychology site.

authors: Neff, L. A., & Karney, B. R.
title: Stress and reactivity to daily relationship experiences: How stress hinders adaptive processes in marriage
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 97(3), 435–450
finding: Spouses under more stress outside the relationship reacted more strongly to everyday negative experiences within it.
strength: moderate — daily-diary studies of newlyweds; correlational
note: The site (book/chapter-3-in-depth.html#leftover) names Neff and Karney without a year; this is the closest-matching paper.

title: The 5 Languages of Appreciation in the Workplace: Empowering Organizations by Encouraging People
finding: Applies the love-languages idea to work: words of affirmation, quality time, acts of service, tangible gifts and appropriate physical touch, with an assessment tool.
strength: early — popular, very little independent testing (as the site says)
note: First published 2011 (Publishers Weekly review June 2011; library catalogues 2011). The site cites it as 2012 — see fixnotes.

authors: Kahn, R. L., Wolfe, D. M., Quinn, R. P., Snoek, J. D., & Rosenthal, R. A.
title: Organizational Stress: Studies in Role Conflict and Ambiguity
finding: Introduced role conflict and role ambiguity as major sources of work stress: not knowing clearly what is expected of you, or facing incompatible demands.
strength: strong — foundational; later meta-analyses link role ambiguity with stress and lower job satisfaction
note: Link is a library catalogue record.

authors: Rizzo, J. R., House, R. J., & Lirtzman, S. I.
title: Role conflict and ambiguity in complex organizations
finding: Developed questionnaire measures of role conflict and role ambiguity, which became the most widely used scales in later research.
strength: strong — measures used in most later role-stress research
note: DOI not confirmed; link is a GESIS bibliographic record.

title: Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 8(4), 377–383
finding: Participants who believed others could also hear a person having a seizure were slower and less likely to help; the presence of others reduced each person’s sense of responsibility.
strength: strong — classic and widely replicated, though weaker in clearly dangerous emergencies

authors: Fischer, P., Krueger, J. I., Greitemeyer, T., Vogrincic, C., Kastenmüller, A., Frey, D., Heene, M., Wicher, M., & Kainbacher, M.
title: The bystander-effect: A meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies
finding: Across 105 effect sizes and over 7,700 participants, the bystander effect was reliable but weaker when situations were clearly dangerous.
strength: strong — large meta-analysis

authors: Latané, B., Williams, K., & Harkins, S.
title: Many hands make light the work: The causes and consequences of social loafing
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(6), 822–832
finding: When clapping and shouting in groups, people put in less individual effort than alone, over and above losses from poor coordination: “social loafing”.
strength: strong — classic, widely replicated

authors: Karau, S. J., & Williams, K. D.
title: Social loafing: A meta-analytic review and theoretical integration
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 65(4), 681–706
finding: Social loafing was reliable across many tasks and populations, and smaller when individual contributions could be identified or evaluated and when the task mattered to people.
strength: strong — meta-analysis
note: DOI matched to title only via an aggregator page; consistent with volume/issue/page from a second listing.

title: Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams
finding: In 51 teams at a manufacturing company, a shared belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks (psychological safety) was linked with more team learning behaviour, which in turn was linked with performance.
strength: strong — highly replicated construct, though most studies are correlational

title: Guide: Understand team effectiveness (Project Aristotle)
finding: Google’s internal research on what makes its teams effective reported that how members interact mattered more than who was on the team, with psychological safety the most important of five factors (with dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and impact).
strength: early — internal company research, not peer-reviewed; findings summarised by Google
note: The re:Work page was confirmed; the “most important factor” ranking was confirmed only through secondary summaries of the guide.

title: Project Retrospectives: A Handbook for Team Reviews
finding: Practitioner handbook on running project retrospectives, including the need for them to feel safe and the “Prime Directive” that everyone did the best job they could with what they knew.
strength: early — practitioner method; evidence comes from wider research on debriefs

authors: Tannenbaum, S. I., & Cerasoli, C. P.
title: Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance? A meta-analysis
finding: Across 46 samples, well-conducted debriefs improved effectiveness by roughly 20–25% on average compared with controls, for both teams and individuals; alignment, facilitation and structure helped.
strength: strong — meta-analysis

title: Human Error
finding: A theory of human error that sorts slips, lapses and mistakes, and introduced the layered-defences thinking behind the “Swiss cheese” model of accidents.
strength: strong — foundational in safety science; the Swiss cheese model is criticised as too simple for complex systems

title: Managing the Risks of Organizational Accidents
finding: Describes how organisational accidents arise from latent conditions combining with front-line errors, and sets out ideas for a safety and “just” culture.
strength: strong — foundational in safety science

title: Just Culture: Balancing Safety and Accountability
finding: Argues for a “just culture” that separates honest mistakes from reckless behaviour, and that who draws the line matters as much as where it is drawn.
strength: moderate — influential practitioner-scholarly book; evidence mainly from case studies
note: Link is a library catalogue record.

authors: Beyer, B., Jones, C., Petoff, J., & Murphy, N. R. (Eds.)
title: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems — Chapter 15, Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure
finding: Describes blameless postmortems: a written record of an incident, its impact, actions taken, root causes and follow-ups, focused on systems rather than blaming individuals.
strength: early — industry practice guide, not research
note: Chapter and URL confirmed; the editors’ names are from general knowledge and were not shown in the search result.

authors: Haynes, A. B., Weiser, T. G., Berry, W. R., et al. (incl. Gawande, A. A.)
title: A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population
finding: In a before-and-after study across eight hospitals in eight cities (7,688 patients), introducing the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist was followed by fewer deaths and major complications.
strength: moderate — large but before-and-after (not randomized); later rollouts showed mixed results

authors: Urbach, D. R., Govindarajan, A., Saskin, R., Wilton, A. S., & Baxter, N. N.
title: Introduction of surgical safety checklists in Ontario, Canada
finding: After surgical checklists were mandated across 101 Ontario hospitals, there was no significant reduction in operative deaths or complications.
strength: moderate — large population study; suggests implementation matters as much as the checklist

authors: Wegner, D. M., Giuliano, T., & Hertel, P. T.
title: Cognitive interdependence in close relationships
venue: In W. J. Ickes (Ed.), Compatible and Incompatible Relationships (pp. 253–276). Springer-Verlag
finding: Proposed that close partners share the work of remembering (“transactive memory”): each relies on the other to know and recall certain things.
strength: moderate — influential theory with supporting experiments in couples and teams

title: Transactive memory: A contemporary analysis of the group mind
venue: In B. Mullen & G. R. Goethals (Eds.), Theories of Group Behavior (pp. 185–208). Springer-Verlag
finding: Defined transactive memory as individual memory systems combined with the communication between people, so a group knows more than any one member.
strength: moderate — foundational theory; supported by later team research
note: Some sources date it 1986; DOI not confirmed.

title: Retrieval processes in transactive memory systems
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(3), 659–671
finding: Dating couples recalled more together than pairs of strangers, consistent with couples using an established system for who remembers what.
strength: moderate — lab experiments with student couples
note: DOI/volume/pages from a reference list that gives the title as “Retrieval processes in transactive memory”; the exact final title (with or without “systems”) should be checked.

authors: Risko, E. F., & Gilbert, S. J.
title: Cognitive offloading
finding: Reviewed how people use physical actions and tools (lists, reminders, notes) to reduce the mental demands of a task, what triggers offloading, and its consequences for memory.
strength: moderate — review of a growing field

authors: Masicampo, E. J., & Baumeister, R. F.
title: Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(4), 667–683
finding: Unfinished goals caused intrusive thoughts and interfered with other tasks; writing a specific plan for the goal removed these effects.
strength: moderate — lab experiments; not yet widely replicated

title: Das Behalten erledigter und unerledigter Handlungen [Remembering completed and uncompleted actions]
finding: Reported that people recalled interrupted tasks better than completed ones.
strength: debated — later studies and a 2025 meta-analysis found the memory effect does not reliably replicate, while the tendency to resume interrupted tasks (Ovsiankina effect) holds up better
note: No DOI confirmed; Wikipedia page used as read-more (it links the original and translations).

title: Interruption, recall and resumption [meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects]
finding: Found no general memory advantage for interrupted tasks (the Zeigarnik effect), but a reliable tendency to resume interrupted tasks (the Ovsiankina effect).
strength: strong — recent meta-analysis
note: First names given as initials from general knowledge; title confirmed only as beginning “Interruption, recall and resumption” — confirm the full title before publishing. Supports the site’s “later reviews” statement.

title: ‘Improving ratings’: Audit in the British University system
finding: Anthropological commentary on the “audit explosion” in British universities; widely credited as the source of the popular phrasing of Goodhart’s law (when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure).
strength: moderate — essay/commentary, widely cited
note: Search did not show the quote itself; it is widely attributed to this paper.

title: Assessing the impact of planned social change
venue: Evaluation and Program Planning (1979); free reprint in Journal of MultiDisciplinary Evaluation, 7(15), 2011
finding: Source of what is called “Campbell’s law”: the more a numerical social indicator is used to make decisions, the more it is open to distortion and the less well it measures what it was meant to.
strength: moderate — widely documented in education, health and business
note: Original 1979 volume/issue/pages from general knowledge, not confirmed; the free reprint (DOI 10.56645/jmde.v7i15.297) is the link. The wording of “Campbell’s law” is from general knowledge.

title: Problems of monetary management: The U.K. experience
venue: Papers in Monetary Economics, Vol. 1, Reserve Bank of Australia
